extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in the UK phone-hacking scandal and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarising arrests, allegations, criticisms and issues arising from the News of the World / News International phone-hacking scandal, and listing the major topics the Leveson Inquiry and other bodies would address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance of the Metropolitan Police Service
rubrics_metrics.description: The Met received severe criticism for its role in the phone hacking scandal; commentators observed that personal relationships among individuals in law enforcement, news media, and political institutions may have compromised principles and judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and concerns listed include: expectations by Met officers of later employment by news organisations possibly compromising relationships; entanglement of personal and commercial interests creating disincentives to thoroughly investigate allegations; failure to notify victims in a timely manner; misleading statements to the public and oversight bodies to cover up wrongdoing; attempts to stifle whistle-blowers; ignoring evidence and conducting anaemic investigations until public disclosure forced action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance of News International
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial investigations by News International had limited objectives and involved pre-screened evidence; outside solicitors were used to produce flawed reports supporting the company's 'rogue reporter' defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The company ultimately acknowledged that News International executives had destroyed evidence and covered up the truth. The text highlights use of flawed internal investigations and the corporate cover-up as central failures to be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance of political leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Political parties' apparent dependence on endorsement by news organisations may have led leaders to turn a blind eye to how newspapers acquired information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: Andy Coulson (former News of the World editor) moved into a senior Conservative Party role and became a high-paid advisor to the prime minister, despite earlier events; parliamentary judgments about Rupert and James Murdoch were made along party lines. The passage suggests potential conflicts of interest and failures of political oversight are issues for consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media coverage of the scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions were raised about whether media coverage was stifled by ownership interests; early coverage by various outlets varied widely, possibly reflecting tension between journalistic integrity and owners' vested interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp) served as a platform for Rupert Murdoch's response; a Fox commentator said 'I'm not going to touch it.' The scandal generated broad international interest after The Guardian's Milly Dowler report; the article notes variability in amount, aggressiveness and focus of early coverage and links to sample media coverage and reference lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulation of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: The UK Press Complaints Commission (PCC) failed to question journalists or editorial executives after Clive Goodman was convicted and accepted the assertion that hacking was a 'rogue' exception; its investigation concluded there was no evidence beyond what had been reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCC report and its conclusions were later withdrawn. The passage frames the PCC's inadequate response and failed self-regulation as a substantive issue to be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Some attempts were made to justify illegal acquisition of confidential information on the basis of public interest, but distinctions were drawn between what is genuinely in the public interest and what is merely interesting to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Amelia Hill (whose reporting helped expose the Milly Dowler hacking) was not prosecuted, while journalists who hacked celebrities claiming public interest were prosecuted. The entry highlights the need to distinguish legitimate public-interest journalism from unlawful intrusion justified by mere public curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting opponents for surveillance
rubrics_metrics.description: News International employed employees and hired private detectives to conduct surveillance beyond phone hacking on targets including a serving police officer investigating agents of News of the World, solicitors representing victims, and a member of parliament critical of the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveillance reportedly included following and videotaping targets and their families (including children), possible phone and computer hacking, searching trash, and opening mail. Some surveillance was proposed by solicitors representing News International allegedly to discredit opponents; the involved solicitor characterised it as 'unusual' but 'justified' and said he 'would do it again tomorrow,' even after News International acknowledged it was 'deeply inappropriate.' This entry details methods and the alleged intent to discredit critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Links to timelines related to the news media phone hacking scandal are included with the phone hacking scandal reference lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that as the wrongdoing's scope widened, related Wikipedia articles and timelines expanded. This entry points readers and investigators to curated chronological resources summarising events and developments.
